compliance.notes: Re-scored on BCP's complete 2026/27 pack after the capital and budget documents were supplied by hand; the earlier assessment_caveat is CLEARED (explicit "") because the capital-strategy content is now in evidence and the residual gaps are BCP's, not ours. BCP publishes no standalone capital strategy: its capital strategy is a section of the Cabinet budget report of 11 February 2026 (paras 66-82, 'The capital strategy is based on the following core principles'), with the Capital Investment Programme (Appendices 7 and 7a) and the 2026-2031 Strategic Asset Management Plan (Appendix 8) as its substance, all recommended to full Council (recommendations viii-x, unchanged by the 10 February addendum). STRONGEST: the liability benchmark (separate General Fund and HRA charts plotting all four balances to 2095); the capital expenditure / financing / CFR chain (five-year GF and HRA tables in the TMS, reconciled to a four-year programme by directorate and by scheme); the borrowing strategy and its candid handling of the projected over-borrowed position driven by cash-flowing the DSG/SEND deficit; the MRP policy (annuity asset-life, £12.8m of VRP overpayments disclosed); the creditworthiness policy (ratings plus a CDS overlay); and the S151 officer's s25 affordability and reserves advice. WEAKEST, and now confirmed as real gaps rather than missing documents: no financing-costs-to-net-revenue-stream ratio for either fund (PI-07), no upper/lower limits on the maturity structure of borrowing (PI-09) and no fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (RISK-02) — three core indicators absent from a 'Treasury Indicators' section that sets only the operational boundary and the authorised limit (and those as a single combined line, in a table headed £'000 whose figures are £m). On the commercial side the supplied capital documents confirm that BCP holds non-treasury investments (investment properties within a £2.16bn estate, council-owned companies and joint ventures, a £15.3m development exposure at Carters Quay) but nowhere quantifies them: no proportionality test against reserves (COM-03, core), no schedule of non-treasury investments by purpose (COM-04), no net commercial/service income ratio (PI-08) and no income-dependence or contingency disclosure (COM-07). Also absent: the promised specified/non-specified investment sections (INV-05), a portfolio risk-exposure indicator (INV-06), any derivatives policy (RISK-06) and any flag on audit qualification of the source data (RPT-05). The Treasury Management Policy, Practices and Schedules document (TMS para 82, 'will be presented alongside') is not in the pack, which limits TMP-01 and GOV-02 but nothing core.

gaps.evidence: TMS p.16 para 80 'The maximum period for investments will be 5 years'; p.15 para 75 sets time limits by counterparty type (local authorities 5 years, Banks 1 higher quality 2 years, Banks 1 medium quality 1 year, DMADF 6 months).
TMS p.10 para 59 reproduces the substance of Prudential Code para 51 and Budget report p.20 para 67 commits every borrowing-funded business case to the PWLB borrowing restrictions.

TMS p.24 Appendix 3: the S151 officer is responsible for 'ensuring the proportionality of all investments so that the Authority does not undertake a level of investing which exposes the Authority to an excessive level of risk compared to its financial resources'; TMS p.6 para 32 asks members, by approving the CFR figures, to 'consider the scale proportionate to the Council's remaining activity'; Budget report p.37 acknowledges exposure to council-owned companies and joint ventures.

news_drafts.headline: BCP Council schools deficit forecast at £275.5m by March 2027, up £95.7m, as SEND plan awaits approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council expects the deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £275.5m by March 2027, up from £179.8m. The first-quarter budget monitoring report, the in-year check of spending against budget, projects an in-year deficit of £95.7m. It says: "At quarter one, the in-year deficit is currently projected to be £95.7m with the cumulative deficit at £275.5m."

The deficit comes from high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The high-needs budget is £68.4m, and the report shows spending more than double that. The council calls the deficit "the Council's biggest financial risk" and the "most significant threat to the Council's long-term financial sustainability".

The council's main response depends on government approval of its local SEND reform plan, submitted in June. The report says the outcome is awaited. If the plan is approved, a High Needs Stability Grant would cover 90% of the deficit as at 31 March 2026, roughly £162m of about £180m, with payment due in autumn 2026. Further support is expected for the 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits. Separately, the capital programme (planned spending on things that last) has £4.59m not yet committed for new Alternative Provision, plus £2.28m across SEND resource schemes. These include £815k at St Clements/St John's, £450k at Pokesdown Primary and £250k at Muscliffe Primary.

news_drafts.headline: BCP Council forecasts £275.5m schools deficit by March 2027; government grant covering 90% awaits approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council expects the accumulated deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £275.5m by March 2027, up from £179.8m at the start of the year. The first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) puts the deficit for 2026/27 alone at £95.7m. It is driven by the cost of placements for children with special educational needs and disabilities, which the council identifies as its most significant financial risk.

A new high needs stability grant, announced in the 2026/27 local government settlement, is intended to cover 90% of the deficit as it stood on 31 March 2026. It depends on government approving the council's local SEND reform plan, which was submitted in June; the outcome is awaited. If approved, the grant would be paid in autumn 2026. Government has also said it expects to offer similar support for further deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, though not without limit, and that from 2028/29 SEND funding is expected to rise to fully fund expected spending.

The reform plan also carries capital spending (money spent on things that last) of £13.5m for 2026/27, made up of £8.9m of high needs grant and £4.6m of Special and Alternative Provision grant. The capital investment report says £4.1m of the high needs grant is "yet to be allocated to specific projects", and the Special and Alternative Provision money is not yet committed to approved schemes. Spending in the first quarter was £163,940. The council expects works to proceed through the summer and autumn holidays.

news_drafts.headline: BCP schools deficit forecast at £275.5m by March 2027; grant for 90% of existing gap awaits approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP) Council expects its deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, to reach £275.5m by 31 March 2027, up from £179.8m a year earlier. A deficit on the grant is an overspend, usually on support for children with special needs. The Schools Forum was told the gap on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), is £95.7m for 2026-27, in line with the original budget. Other parts of the grant are forecast to balance.

The government has offered a stability grant covering 90% of the deficit at 31 March 2026, about £161.8m, to be paid in autumn 2026 if approved. It depends on government approval of BCP's local SEND reform plan, submitted in June; the outcome is awaited. The government has said there should be no further deficits beyond March 2028, as funding from 2028-29 rises to cover expected spending, with details due in the 2027 Spending Review. A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such a deficit off the council's main balance sheet, also runs until 31 March 2028.

The yearly gap has grown from £49.7m in 2024-25 to £71.6m in 2025-26. Spending on independent and non-maintained special schools has risen from £30.2m to £49.3m over the period. The reform plan aims to shift investment towards early intervention, and a newly established High Needs Block Board oversees the deficit recovery plan.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Council's IT infrastructure at end of supported lifecycle, creating cyber security exposure and service disruption risk without planned investment
findings.detail: The Council's IT infrastructure and laptop estate is reaching end of supported lifecycle, creating increasing cyber security exposure, reducing system reliability and increasing the likelihood of service disruption and reactive maintenance costs as assets become unsupported. Without structured replacement investment, the Council faces rising maintenance costs, reduced system performance and higher risks to delivery of critical services. This asset condition provides the operational and financial justification for the £11.2m lifecycle-based investment programme.
findings.matters: Asset end-of-life condition and cyber security risk justify the investment; understanding the drivers is essential to assess whether the investment reduces or increases the Council's financial risk profile.
findings.figures: Infrastructure serving approximately 6,500 users across multiple sites
findings.quote: BCP Council's IT infrastructure and laptop estate is now reaching the end of its supported lifecycle, creating increasing challenges in maintaining performance, supportability and compatibility with delivery of modern systems and services.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: £0.5 million approved in May 2026 for early laptop purchase to lock in prices before anticipated cost increase of approximately £500 per device
findings.detail: In May 2026, the Council approved £498,200 capital expenditure for early purchase of 470 Microsoft Surface Laptop devices at £1,060 per device under delegated officer authority, ahead of full Council approval for the remaining programme funding. This procurement decision shows the Council actively managing technology cost inflation risks; the anticipated £500-per-device price increase reflects market cost volatility that could affect the assumptions underpinning the wider £11.2m investment plan.
findings.matters: Shows the Council is actively managing technology cost inflation risks within a larger capital programme; the anticipated price pressure signals market cost volatility that may affect programme cost assumptions.
findings.figures: £498,200 approved May 2026; 470 devices at £1,060 per device; anticipated future increase of approximately £500 per device
findings.quote: The decision was taken to secure a favourable price and avoid an anticipated increase of approximately £500 per device.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Council seeking approval for £11.2 million prudential borrowing over six years to fund IT infrastructure investment from 2026 to 2032
findings.detail: Cabinet is seeking approval to recommend to Council approval of prudential borrowing of £11.2m for a lifecycle-based IT infrastructure capital investment programme. The borrowing requires £2.8m revenue allocation over the 6-year period to repay the debt: £1.1m is already factored into the Medium-Term Financial Plan and £1.7m requires further MTFP growth. This structure recognises the revenue implications of the borrowing commitment and embeds repayment into the Council's financial planning.
findings.matters: A significant new prudential borrowing commitment with identified revenue implications signals both necessary capital investment and creates budget pressure to find additional funding beyond current plans.
findings.figures: £11.2 million borrowing; £2.8 million revenue cost over 6 years; £1.1 million already in MTFP; £1.7 million requires further MTFP growth
findings.quote: Recommend to Audit and Governance Committee to recommend to council to approve prudential borrowing of £11.2m to support delivery of the programme over 6 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Cost forecasts for later programme years (2030-2032) subject to greater uncertainty due to IT market volatility and emerging technology cost pressures
findings.detail: Council's assessment: confidence in cost estimates is strongest for 2027/28-2028/29 where requirements defined and prices known. For later years (2030-2032), uncertainty increases due to pace of technological change, rapid growth in artificial intelligence and data-driven services, escalating cyber security requirements, and external market factors. Council will manage through annual refinement of cost profiles.
findings.matters: Signals that 6-year forecast may underestimate outturn, particularly for cyber security and emerging technology requirements, creating potential budget pressure in final two years of the programme.
findings.figures: Uncertainty flagged for 2030/31 (£1.721m) and 2031/32 (£1.400m); interest rate forecasts step down 4.8% to 4.1% across same period
findings.quote: As the programme progresses into later years, there is a greater degree of uncertainty, reflecting the inherent pace of change within the technology sector and the influence of external market factors.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 IT & Programmes Infrastructure Capital Investment Plan 2026 2032
findings.headline: Total borrowing cost of £2.8m over 6 years, adding £1.7m net new growth to medium-term financial plan
findings.detail: Based on PWLB rates of 5.34% as of 9 June 2026, forecast to step down to 4.8% (year 1), 4.2% (year 2), and 4.1% (years 3-6), over 5-year borrowing period. £1.1m borrowing cost already included in existing MTFP; net new cost growth to MTFP is therefore £1.7m. Interest rate assumptions signal council expects PWLB rates to decline.
findings.matters: Shows forward impact on medium-term budgets and council's assessment of interest rate direction; material to any lender monitoring debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: £2.8m total borrowing cost; £1.1m existing MTFP; £1.7m net new MTFP growth; 5.34% PWLB rate (9 June 2026); 4.8%, 4.2%, 4.1% forecast rates
findings.quote: The total cost of prudential borrowing for the £11.2 million investment over 6 years is £2.8 million. As £1.1 million is already reflected in the MTFP, the growth from MTFP perspective is £1.7 million.
